title: The Non-Freaked Out, Focused Approach to the Common Core
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: This is the founding post of Stuart's 'non-freaked out' series, in which a self-described former standards-avoider argues that the CCSS literacy standards can be boiled down to a handful of high-leverage priorities. He rejects two responses he sees around him: panicked, fear-driven implementation, and the calm but equally unhelpful choice to ignore the standards altogether. His filter is one question: which standards are most likely to prepare science, social studies, and ELA students to flourish after 12th grade? That yields six priorities: much more grade-level complex text, whole-class instruction in closely reading it, a heavy emphasis on argument, every student speaking every day, writing constantly, and explicit teaching of grit and self-control. For each he describes concrete classroom practice - think-pair-share and random cold-calling, PVLEGS delivery rubrics, model essays, and grading only a fraction of student writing. He argues that character strengths are what make the demanding academic work possible, and he openly admits that he is cutting wide swaths of the standards.
points: Stuart argues that praising students who only enjoy self-selected reading can 'kill them softly', because it implies that loving books is enough for post-secondary life without the ability to grapple with difficult or boring texts.

Complex text only works when it is paired with instruction: modeling, vocabulary, annotation, and checks for understanding (after Schmoker's Focus) are what make R.CCR.10 achievable for a ninth grader reading at a fifth-grade level.
He treats argument in the Graff tradition as collaborative rather than combative, a way to 'get to the bottom of things', and reports that it draws reluctant readers into complex texts.

His writing workload solution is to have students write far more than he grades: he only glances at provisional writing, responds to about a quarter of readable writing, and gives polished pieces one or two focused targets.
He places grit and self-control among the standards themselves, on the argument that the Common Core's demands become 'infinitely harder and more pointless' without them.
quotes: When I set out in June 2012 to blog through the Common Core State Standards (CCSS), I was, as long-time readers know, a diehard standards avoider. To me, standards were nothing more than codified wish lists created by committees. They were useful for getting good grades on School of Ed lesson plans, and that was the extent of their value.

As many readers have shared elsewhere on the blog, Common Core implementation throughout the US has been largely accomplished with scarce amounts of grace and heaping portions of fear, stress, and ignorance. Too few teachers are given paid PD time to simply read and process the CCSS as professionals, and even less are being trusted to determine with their colleagues what from the Standards is worth their focus.

In other words, I'm not content to see some of my students reading 600 pages of self-selected reading per week while being unable to grapple with difficult (even, dare I say it, boring) tasks. If I unreservedly praise such “lifelong readers,” I kill them softly, effectively saying, “Hey, all it takes to flourish in life is to love reading.

It's pointless to give students grade-level complex texts if we don't empower students with simple, effective instructional practices like modeling, vocabulary instruction, annotating, and checks for understanding (Mike Schmoker's Focus is baller at explaining this). That's why, to me, R.CCR.1 is the perfect complement to R.CCR.10.

One key reason that so many undervalue argument is because they associate it with anger and discord. But argument proper is something that can actually bring us together and, as one author puts it, helps us collaboratively “get to the bottom of things.

Because I never hand back copiously corrected papers to students, they get their work back faster with 1-2 things to work on for next time. This allows us to write like crazy without having me go crazy.

I will be surprised if non-cognitive skills (my students and I refer to them as character strengths) do not gain a large share of the ed reform conversation in the decade to come. A big reason that most of my students are willing to tread the demanding paths of complex texts, close reading, arguing, mandatory speaking, and writing is because they are growing in their skills of grit and self-control.
